For what reason did the Blessed One not state that craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and grasping (*upādāna*)—the two types that produce [existence]—serve as conditions for formative forces (*saṃskāra*)?
The World-Honored One replied:
"Craving and grasping both operate within their own respective realms;
because they have a limited scope, [they do not extend beyond them]."
Why is this? Because craving and grasping in the desire realm [lead to] those various imperturbable formations in the form realm or the formless realm.
It is not logical for it to serve as a condition of origination (*samutthāna-pratyaya*),
because it is not its object (*ālambana*).

Furthermore, it is stated that ignorance serves as a productive condition for the arising of [karmic formations] belonging to the desire realm or the form realm that are free from passion (*vītarāga*).
It acts as the motivating condition (*samutthāna-pratyaya*). Furthermore,
it is said that this ignorance is accompanied by the improper mental attention (*ayoniśo-manasikāra*) arising from it and its results.
It can serve as the condition for the formations (*saṃskāra*) of that realm, such as the immovable (*āneñjya*).
This means that ignorance (*avidyā*) of one realm serves as the condition for the formations of another realm.
If, having attained a member (*aṅga*) of one realm, one subsequently gives rise to a member of another realm—
How, then, is the statement in the *Pañcāśikā* to be reconciled? It says:
"In whatever realm or stage one is born, it should be understood that the members of existence (*bhavāṅga*) are subsumed within that very [realm or stage]."
Treatise:
Regarding the various members of dependent origination up to the initiation of practice for a higher stage.
Commentary states:
This is the sixth question.
All members of dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda) rely upon their own respective levels (bhūmi).
This is consistent with fifty-six textual passages.
There is an active manifestation that, depending on the ignorance of others, functions as a common condition for dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*). What is this like?
Its specific nature should now be clarified.
Is it one or many? This is only one,
just as ignorance of a lower stage gives rise to formations of a higher stage.
Treatise:
It is not so, because from the initial subduing until [the afflictions] have not yet arisen.
Commentary says:
It is not permitted that ignorance belonging to a lower stage gives rise to a practice (*caryā*) of a higher stage.

If one has merely suppressed the defilements of a lower stage but has not yet attained a meditative absorption (*dhyāna*) of a higher stage, then that [state] should not be considered the "limb of practice" (*saṃskāra-aṅga*).
In order to enter that fundamental meditative absorption,
one must first abandon the nine grades of desire;
only at a later time does the ignorance of that stage subsequently arise.
At that time, because ignorance has not yet arisen in that stage,
that contaminated concentration (*sāsrava-samādhi*) should not be a member of the formative forces (*saṃskāra-aṅga*),
as the member of ignorance would be absent.

Since it is named a "limb of volitional formations" (*saṃskāra-anga*), it is clear that it is produced by ignorance (*avidyā*). This meaning demonstrates that the fifty-sixth [treatise] speaks based on the explanation of multiple limbs;
the intent of the Sūtra is to provide a comprehensive discussion.
There is reliance upon other stages,
and there is no contradiction either;
this text can clarify that the *anāgamya* stage is free from afflictions.
The root [affliction] cannot be attained,
because it never arises;
it is merely that which arises from below.
The *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* states that from the initial arising until one has not yet reached [the higher stage],
it all proceeds in this manner; from the upper and lower stages, one arises and gives rise to the link of craving (*tṛṣṇā*).
The commentary states:
This seventh question proceeds from the higher to the lower.
Arising from the lower stage toward the upper stage,
that craving capable of moistening what is to be born takes as its condition the limb of feeling belonging to whichever level it belongs to.
Is it the stage where one is to be born,
or the stage where one currently dwells?
For what reason is this question asked?
Since craving arises conditioned by feeling,
and because the present arising of the limb of feeling and the future craving belong to different stages (bhūmi),
it should be admitted— just as with the projection of karma by ignorance— that they can be established as belonging to different stages.
In response to this question, the treatise states:
"That craving also takes as its object [the Truths], which is not contrary to principle."
The commentary states:
According to what is appropriate,
that craving also takes as its object the sensation of the place where one is to be reborn.
Whether it be feeling manifesting simultaneously or feeling as a seed from a prior time,
there is no contradiction in principle.

Regarding the statement here that "it also takes as its object the feeling of the place where one will be born," this clarifies that when dying in one’s own stage and being reborn in one’s own stage, craving necessarily relies on the same stage;
likewise, when being reborn in a different stage from the one of death, it also necessarily relies on the same stage [of that new birth].
Therefore, it is said that "likewise.
Furthermore, the experience of one's current dwelling place also serves as a condition for craving.

Just as that ignorance serves as a condition for a different stage (*bhūmi*), this [ignorance] is not a member of the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-aṅga*), though it possesses the sense of being a remote condition (*viprakṛṣṭa-pratyaya*). Question: The afflictions that incite karma serve as conditions for a different stage.

The delusions that moisten rebirth (*upapatti-saṃyojana*) should likewise belong to different stages. Answer: The arousal of karma (*karma-samutthāna*) is the cause of equal origination (*samutthāna-hetu*);
because it is remote, it extends across different stages.
Moistening rebirth is the cause of actual production (*janana-hetu*).
Question: Since feeling conditions craving, it may extend to other stages;
since volitional formations condition consciousness, they may serve as conditions for other stages. Answer: Feeling conditions craving as a remote cause.
Because they are remote, [the formations] extend across different levels (*bhūmi*). Since formations take consciousness as their object, they are ripening causes (*vipāka-hetu*).
Because they are proximate, [they belong] only to their own level. Question: For what reason are consciousness and the others [treated thus]?
Regarding birth and so forth, there are different ways of classifying them as either distinct or combined.

In this case, "volitional formations" (*saṃskāra*) and "existence" (*bhava*) are both combined into one. Answer: Volitional formations refer to karma that exists as a projecting cause (*ākṣepa-hetu*) and is characterized by creative activity.
Craving and grasping, moistened [by them], are designated as "existence" (*bhava*);

they have no separate substantial entity, and therefore they are not distinguished from one another. Question: If existence were merely karma, it would be identical to the "formations" (*saṃskāra*) alone.
Question: Since there are [factors] that pertain to existence (*bhava*) yet are neither karma nor non-karma, why are they not mentioned? Answer:

Although among those pertaining to existence there are both karma and non-karma, because both are equally proximate to the fruit of future existence (*punar-bhava*), their force and significance are balanced.
These are collectively termed "existence" (*bhava*).

It is not that [the preceding stage] is excluded because, like "formations" (*saṃskāra*), it does not lack the nature of karma. Question: Why is that which has not yet been moistened called "formations," while that which has already been moistened is called "existence"?
Answer: That which performs an action is called "formation."
Because the meaning of "initial formation" is manifested,
the first is called "volitional formations" (*saṃskāra*).
That which possesses a fruit is called "existence" (*bhava*).

Because they are moistened before being projected, the latter is established as "existence" (bhava). Question: Why are the three types of karma collectively termed "formations" (saṃskāra), while existence and the defilements that moisten them are both termed "craving" (tṛṣṇā)?

Regarding the division into craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and grasping (*upādāna*): [the former] moistens the fruit so that it does not arise; [the latter] constitutes the union of karma capable of producing the fruit.
Thus, craving and grasping are divided into two.
One karma is able to induce the convergence of the fruit.
The establishment of practice has its name.
Regarding the nine concentrations that refute heterodoxy,
there are the Sarvāstivādins and others.
Two causes and five fruits;
three causes and two fruits;
these are definitely not of the same time period.
Now, within this school, the treatise states:
"These twelve links are each fixed to the same world-period (*adhvan*)."
The commentary states:
The first ten factors are the causes,
and the final two factors are the results.
It is certain that they do not belong to the same lifetime,
because the general ripening cause does not entail that the very body which performed the action immediately receives its fruit.
Furthermore, it is not the case that present karma obtains its fruit [within the same lifetime], because this pertains to the twelve links [of dependent origination].
With respect to the death and birth of the body,
the ten causes and two fruits are definitively distinct.
If considered in terms of temporal divisions,
this is indeterminate; for example,
as with karma to be experienced in subsequent lives, one may have performed the first seven [types of karma] in the past.
Subsequently, as long as the future body is not yet matured, craving and grasping do not arise in the present body;
rather, they arise only when that future body is ready,
whereby one experiences the fruit in successive future births.
Is it not because craving (*tṛṣṇā*), grasping (*upādāna*), birth (*jāti*), and old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*) all reside in the future,
that the three time periods are explained here according to the broad divisions of time?

The meaning is not yet fixed; what is being discussed here takes the cycle of birth and death within a single lifetime as its temporal framework. Among these, the first seven branches of the causal phase correspond to craving, grasping, and becoming.
Either in a different lifetime or in the same lifetime,
such as karma to be experienced upon rebirth (upapadyavedanīya-karma).
At the time of one's first birth,
that world must be the same;
from the second birth onward, it may differ.
This continues up to the karma of future retribution;
the worlds are not the same.
This is because craving and grasping only arise when one is about to experience the fruit of the karma created in this life, at a later or even subsequent stage.
According to the Sārvastivāda masters, craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and grasping (*upādāna*) have three [aspects].
These are definitely not of the same time period as the first two of the seven types mentioned previously.
The [remaining] five members are necessarily co-existent with their acquisition (*prāpti*),
because one gives rise to afflictions and performs karma during the stages of birth, aging, and death in a previous life.
Thus, within this context, these twelve links are necessarily co-existent.
That is to say: birth and old age and death constitute two [links];
craving, grasping, and existence constitute three;
and ignorance and the other preceding seven [constitute the remaining seven].
Each is determined to belong to the same lifetime.
Because karma produced through delusion necessarily perfumes the seeds of retribution within the same lifetime,
the first seven links cannot belong to different lifetimes.
The water of arising afflictions moistens the previous six types [of existence], which then transform and are termed "becoming" (*bhava*).
This also does not occur at a different time;
it is not the case that the moisture arises at one time and the moistened object is established only at a later, separated time.
Birth and old age-and-death are known to belong to the same world;
therefore, these two, three, and seven [factors] are each fixed as belonging to the same world.
This is what constitutes being fixed in time.
Ten members are causes;
two members are results.
The cause exists in the past.
The fruit is either in the present or in the future,
while the cause is in the present.
If one speaks in terms of the fruit in the future life,
it is discussed as occurring across two lifetimes; however, according to the principle of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), it also involves three lifetimes.
The ten causes of the past have two fruits in the present;
the two fruits of the future have ten causes in the present.
This constitutes the twelvefold dependent origination across two time periods.
It may also be said that they belong to the three periods of time (*tri-kāla*). Generally speaking, because two of the periods are not fixed, they may be considered to span all three periods.
If the first seven [members] are situated in the past, [the others follow accordingly].
Craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and grasping (*upādāna*) exist in the present;
birth (*jāti*) and old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*)—these two—exist in the future.
Thus, the twelve links (*dvādaśāṅga*) span all three periods of time.
That is, the twelve links, whether spanning two lifetimes or three lifetimes,
involve karma being created by one body and karma being moistened by another body.
Therefore, this differs from the Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna), which holds that two causes are past, five fruits are present, three causes are present, and two fruits are future.
The temporal sequence of dependent origination is definitively established in this manner.
The *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle eight:
On the twelvefold dependent origination,
extending even to the dependent origination spanning the three periods of time.
Those who equate this with the Hīnayāna have translated it erroneously; now, having consulted the Sanskrit original,
it is found that it agrees with the *Yogācārabhūmi* and other texts, which speak only of the three time periods (*trikāla*).
This refers to dependent origination from the prior limit to the middle limit,
and from the middle limit to the subsequent limit;

for it is ignorance that is deluded regarding the principles of the truths (*satya*),
whose activity is predominant and capable of projecting [karmic formations].
This is the first reason.
Furthermore, both the sūtras and the śāstras state that noble ones (ārya) necessarily do not create karma for future existence;
this is the second reason.
If ignorance were to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*),
then noble ones (*ārya*) would have to create karma anew;
for the *Abhidharma* (Dharmapada-skandha-pāda-śāstra), chapter seven, states that both types of delusion (*moha*) are abandoned through seeing (*darśana-heya*).
It is said that those who have already seen the Truth do not create meritorious or immovable formations because they lack delusion regarding the true meaning. Some explain it as follows:

The delusion regarding maturation (*vipāka-moha*) is abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), while the delusion regarding the true meaning (*tattvārtha-moha*) is abandoned through the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*). This reasoning is not correct,
for it is stated later in the *Pratītyasamutpādādivibhaṅganirdeśa*:
Ordinary beings outside the Buddhist fold initiate action through four types of ignorance and fully perform the three kinds of karma, such as non-meritorious karma;
ordinary beings within the Buddhist fold, excluding the unique ignorance, have formations conditioned by the remaining three types of ignorance.
The practice of those who are heedful does not have ignorance as its condition.
Furthermore, the Abhidharma states:
Delusion regarding maturation gives rise to non-meritorious formations;
delusion regarding the true nature of reality gives rise to meritorious and immovable formations.
If the delusions abandoned through cultivation are first [abandoned] and the delusions abandoned through seeing are later [abandoned],
how could it be that the afflictions distinguished by the path of seeing produce only merit and the imperturbable?
Regarding the delusions of those practicing the path,
do they give rise to non-merit?
This is explained in the fifty-ninth [treatise].
The karma that projects rebirth in the three evil destinies arises solely from conceptualized afflictions,
not from innate afflictions.
Could it be that the non-meritorious formations and ignorance which give rise [to rebirth] are abandoned through the path of cultivation?
If you say they give rise to karma of distinct retribution, [then how can they be abandoned by the path of seeing]?
It would then not be a factor of the path of action;
it would instead be the delusion regarding the karma that produces the general retribution for the evil destinies.
In reality, it is abandoned only by insight (*darśana-prahātavya*).
Why, then, is it said that ignorance regarding maturation (*vipāka-moha*) is abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*)?
Furthermore, there are two explanations regarding this:
[first,] the ignorance that actually initiates karma; [second,]...

Because they are abandoned only by the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*), that person further says: one is deluded regarding the first seven sufferings through ignorance of maturation (*vipāka-moha*), while one is deluded regarding the eighth suffering through ignorance of the true meaning (*tattvārtha-moha*).
The *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle ten, states:
Delusion regarding conventional suffering gives rise to non-meritorious [karma];
delusion regarding ultimate suffering gives rise to meritorious and immovable [karma].
The sixth chapter of the Abhidharma states:
The first seven types of suffering are conventional suffering;
the eighth type of suffering is ultimate suffering.
Therefore, it gives rise to non-meritorious ignorance (*apuṇyāvidyā*).
This is abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*). It is not so for the others, which are abandoned through the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*).
How could it be [the same] merely because the conventional expression "suffering" is identical?
The phrasing "in all places" refers to this single conventional [truth].
It is called "conventional" because it is easily understood;
it is called "ultimate" because it is the domain of supreme wisdom alone.
That which is called the fruit of non-merit is easily known by worldly people to be suffering;
thus it is termed "worldly suffering."
Merit and the fruit of immovability—
only through superior wisdom does one realize these as suffering;
this is called suffering in the ultimate sense (paramārtha-duḥkha).
It is not that suffering is divided into eight parts;
rather, within those eight sufferings, there are what are termed the conventional and the ultimate.
The first seven are easy to understand and are termed conventional;
the eighth is known by superior wisdom (*viśeṣajñāna*).
This is called the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
It does not mean that the preceding seven are conventional truths (*saṃvṛti*) consisting of deluded, non-meritorious actions.
If it were otherwise, [the following would occur].
Among the first seven types of suffering,
the sixth and seventh are the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkha*).
Is it not the case that the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) and others lack the suffering of change?
If such [a self] existed,
why would one who is deluded not create non-meritorious karma?
Furthermore, could there not be an eighth kind of ultimate suffering within the miserable realms?
For what reason does one who is deluded therein perform only meritorious and immovable karma?
Thus we know that identical phrasing does not necessarily imply a single meaning;
in this context, ignorance is exclusively abandoned through insight (*darśana-prahātavya*).
These interrogations are explained in detail in a separate chapter. The treatise states:
"The two factors of craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and grasping (*upādāna*) extend to those abandoned through seeing (*darśana-heya*) and cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*)."
The commentary states:
According to the intention of the first master,
craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and grasping (*upādāna*) are abandoned only through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).
The craving that seeks rebirth and moistens rebirth is clearly not abandoned by insight (*darśana-prahātavya*),
because craving and the like abandoned by insight arise conditioned by insight and so forth.
The *Abhidharmasamuccaya* (Treatise on the Dharma) states that there are nine types of death-minds (*cyuti-citta*).
This is because for each of the three realms,
there are three types of birth-sustaining minds (*pratisandhi-citta*) that moisten rebirth within those respective realms.
He says that innate craving and innate ignorance are abandoned only through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*);
the link of grasping (*upādāna*) is merely a predominance of craving and does not refer to the four types of grasping.
Regarding the "four graspings" (*catvāry upādānāni*): in a general sense, the meaning of "grasping" is not subsumed under the specific link of grasping (*upādānāṅga*).
The remaining nine [defilements] are abandoned through both the path of vision (*darśana-mārga*) and the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*).
Because they are severed by means of the causes of karma,
those indeterminate dharmas are not severed solely through cultivation;
this shall be understood further below.
Treatise:
There is an interpretation that all [afflictions] do not reach total severance.
The commentary states:
Within the second master’s [position], there are three parts:
first, the statement of the thesis;
second, the presentation of the objection.
"Third, revealing the correct [view]: all [factors] pertain to both types of abandonment;
this is the statement of the thesis. From 'The treatise says' onwards, the two difficulties are addressed."
These twelve links are all, without exception, subject to abandonment through both the path of seeing and the path of cultivation.
With what intention [is it said] that ignorance is also abandoned through the path of cultivation,
and that the two links of craving and grasping are also abandoned through the path of seeing?

The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, in its tenth [chapter], states that those who have attained the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpanna*) have severed one portion of all the links of dependent origination (*bhavāṅga*), but not all of them entirely. Thus says the treatise.
"If the factor of ignorance has not been completely severed," the commentary states,
[this] is a challenge to the previous master.
If the factor of ignorance were to be abandoned solely by the path of seeing,
then the stream-enterer would have completely abandoned that first factor;
how then could it be said that for a stream-enterer there is no complete abandonment?
Regarding the statement that "it severs one portion of all factors of existence" (*bhavāṅga*), the treatise says:
"If the factors of craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and grasping (*upādāna*) reach one portion of all factors."
The commentary states:
Furthermore, there is an objection:
if, according to the former master, the members of craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and grasping (*upādāna*) are abandoned only through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).
It should rather be said that for one who has attained the stream-entry (srotāpanna),

all factors (aṅga) have been abandoned except for a portion of the two factors of craving (tṛṣṇā) and grasping (upādāna), which are not abandoned by the path of vision (darśanamārga) because they are not [wholly] present.
Nor is it even a partial [cessation], because it has not been abandoned at all.
If they were to offer this defense: "The tenth chapter of the *Mahā-śāstra* merely relies on a general statement and speaks from the perspective of the majority."
Treatise:
Furthermore, it is said that all afflictions throughout the realms can give rise [to karma].
Commentary: [As follows:]
If that is so, how do [the treatises] state in the fifty-ninth [verse] and elsewhere that all afflictions (*kleśa*) of the entire realm (*dhātu*) are capable of linking rebirth (*pratisaṃdhi*)?
The term "linking rebirth" indicates the delusions that moisten birth (*upapatti-śleṣa-kleśa*).

If it were only through cultivation that [the defilements] moisten [rebirth], then because the afflictions of the path of vision within the realms do not moisten rebirth, they would not be called "belonging to all realms.
This objection applies to craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and grasping (*upādāna*), which are abandoned only through cultivation.
Furthermore, it is stated that the link of grasping (*upādāna*) comprehensively includes the four types of grasping;
this is because views (*dṛṣṭi*), attachment to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), and so forth, are not abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).
The following objection [is raised] at the beginning of the fifty-ninth [verse] regarding the claim that ignorance (*avidyā*) is abandoned solely through insight (*darśana-heya*).
Furthermore, it is stated that the conduct leading to the evil destinies is incited solely by afflictions arising from conceptual construction;
thus, one should likewise say that the conduct leading to birth in the five destinies is incited solely by afflictions arising from conceptual construction.
This is because the abandonment of afflictions through insight does not merely give rise to conduct leading to the evil destinies.
If it is argued that the karma which brings about distinct retributions for humans and devas can be incited by the afflictions of cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), [the response follows].
Because it is explained by way of both general and specific retributions,
the treatise does not state that those who produce rebirth as humans or devas [commit] karma that results specifically in the miserable realms.

The afflictions of the path of cultivation (bhāvanā-heya) should not give rise to [rebirth]; yet they do give rise to the karma that leads to the specific retribution of the miserable destinies (durgati). Since the afflictions of the path of cultivation are indeed capable of giving rise [to such results], [the distinction between the two types of karma must be maintained].
Therefore, it is known that his statement concerns only the total retribution (*vipāka*).
The treatise does not say that [the karma] moistens birth or issues forth until the stage of what is abandoned by seeing (*darśana-heya*).
The commentary states:
Among the various sacred teachings, it is not said that the delusions which moisten rebirth are exclusively abandoned through cultivation,
because the afflictions of all realms are capable of effecting the linking of rebirth.
Nor does it state that all formations which induce future existence are produced by what is abandoned through seeing; rather,
it says only that the formations leading to the miserable destinies are produced by the afflictions of conceptual discrimination.
Treatise:
From this, it is known that [this applies] up to what is abandoned through seeing and cultivation. Commentary:
The conclusion establishing the correct principle has two parts:
first, the conclusion regarding the three members;
second, a general explanation of the refutation.
The first of these [three] consists of the three links of ignorance, craving, and grasping;
these are also to be abandoned through both insight and cultivation.
Regarding the seven factors of the Dharma, the treatise states:
"However, as for the factor of ignorance leading to its auxiliaries, it is not fixed."
The commentary states:
Those that are correctly activated are abandoned solely by insight (*darśana-prahātavya*),
because they are coarse and violent.
Therefore, it is said that both types of delusion are abandoned through the path of seeing (*darśana-heya*).
The *Fifty-nine [Discourses]* states that their "auxiliaries" are not fixed,
because the karma that assists in producing the general retribution of humans and devas also extends to the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*).
He merely states that it is the act of generating rebirth in the miserable realms;
only the afflictions of conceptual discrimination can assist in generating the collective retribution for rebirth in the miserable realms.

Because most [unwholesome states] are abandoned only through seeing (*darśana-prahātavya*), the production of distinct retributions (*vipāka*) and so forth are also, for the most part, abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*);
this is stated according to the majority.
This is not contradictory.
The *Huìduìfǎ* (Confrontation of Dharmas), fascicle six, regarding "moistening birth," states:
"That which truly moistens birth is exclusively abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*)."
Because it manifests with subtle frequency,
that [text] speaks only of its association with innate craving (*sahaja-tṛṣṇā*);
therefore, the auxiliary factor is not fixed.
Therefore, it is said that all afflictions throughout the entire realm are capable of linking rebirth,
and that the four types of grasping are all designated as the "grasping" limb (*upādāna-aṅga*) and so forth.
However, the defilements that initiate karma exist only as seeds.
Just as for an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) who is not negligent regarding internal phenomena,
those afflictions that moisten rebirth exist only as seeds;
this refers to a non-returner (*anāgāmin*).
Some say that this refers to those who have died from the state of non-perception (*asaṃjñika*),
based on the primary activation and primary moistening [of the seeds].
However, there is no fault in admitting that [seeds] arise through auxiliary activation and auxiliary moistening even in the present life.
Because remote causes (*dūre-hetv-utthāna*) also exist in the present;
and because manifest afflictions (*vartamāna-kleśa*) arise even before the end of life.
Question: It is now stated that all twelve [factors] are common to both the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) and the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*).
How can it be said that the meaning of "abandonment" applies to that [state]? The treatise states:
Furthermore, because defiled phenomena are permanently abandoned upon reaching that [state].
The commentary states:
The following provides a general explanation of the meaning of "all abandonment.
This seed of the dharmas of darkness is in opposition to those dharmas of untainted luminosity.
When the untainted [state] arises, the seeds of darkness are severed.
Since the nature of form is not defiled,
this severance applies universally to all minds and mental factors.
Treatise:
All contaminated phenomena (sāsrava) do not contradict the Path. Commentary:
[As stated above].
Non-defiled dharmas refer to those that are wholesome and non-obscured neutral; they are not,
by their very nature, subject to abandonment.
Its essence is not a dharma of darkness;
it thus pervades the five aggregates,
for it does not contradict the Path.
Treatise:
However, there are two meanings regarding how one comes to be associated with those afflictions.
Commentary states:
However, this wholesome and indeterminate [state] is said to be "abandoned" for two reasons: first, abandonment by way of dissociation from bondage (*visamyoga-prahāṇa*).
That is to say: the abandonment of those afflictions which take it as their object,
those afflictions mixed with it,
and those afflictions that take it as their object.
This refers to those with outflows (*sāsrava*) that arise conditioned by afflictions;

they consist of the objects of the seven consciousnesses, such as wholesome states and so forth, which possess outflows. If one eliminates the afflictions that take these as their objects, [the consciousnesses cease].
To speak of the objects of perception is to say that they have been severed.
As for "those afflictions being mixed with it," this refers to when the seventh consciousness gives rise to afflictions.
Although the six consciousnesses and other such phenomena do not take that [storehouse consciousness] as their object-condition,
the six consciousnesses and others become of a tainted nature by virtue of it,
because it is called the "basis of defilement."
Within the states of the three natures (trisvabhāva), those afflictions of the six consciousnesses and so forth arise constantly.

When the afflictions of the seventh [consciousness] are severed, the dharmas of the six consciousnesses and so forth are said to have attained severance. Furthermore, that which arises intermittently is termed "mixed" (vyavakīrṇa).
This interpretation implies that there are the Wisdom of Equality and the others,
because afflictions such as those of the seventh consciousness arise intermittently.
However, when [factors] are concordant with one another, they are termed "intermingled" (*miśra*).
The sixth [category] is untainted (*anāsrava*), and the seventh does not accord with the afflictions (*kleśa*);
because they are directly opposed to them, they are not called "mixed.
These are not the causal motivations (*hetu-samutthāna*).
Because various neutral (*avyākṛta*) karmas do not arise from a causal motivation (*hetu-samutthāna*), they are merely interspersed; yet there is still the sense of "intermixture.
Since their nature is conducive to the outflows (*āsrava*), their intermittent arising is termed "mixed."
Furthermore, regarding "mixed":

this refers to wholesome contaminated (*sāsrava*) karma, which, because it is induced by afflictions (*kleśa*), takes on a contaminated nature and is thus not the same as the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
Furthermore, at the time when those [defilements] are severed, the wholesome [states] are also said to be severed. Moreover, it is explained that the mind bound by association,
as well as the nature of the universal [mental factors] and so forth— which are not themselves defiled dharmas—
are called "bound by afflictions" because they coexist with the afflictions.
When the afflictions are severed,
that mind-king, along with its universal mental factors and so forth, is said to attain severance,
because it has become dissociated from the associated delusions.
This is called "severing those defilements that are mixed with it.
Although the sovereign mind (citta-rāja), the universal mental factors (sarvatraga), and so forth, are associated with defiled phenomena, [they are not themselves defiled].

Because its nature is not a dharma to be abandoned (*prahātavya*), it is included in this category; this interpretation contradicts the subsequent passage stating that [afflictions] are abandoned only through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).
How could there be no associated fetters (*saṃprayukta-bandhana*) in the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*)?
From this, one should understand.
The first two explanations are correct.
If one speaks of the seven consciousnesses as being associated with various afflictions,
this refers to those who have abandoned the nine grades of desire but have not yet attained the state of an Aśaikṣa.
Wholesome states of the desire realm and so forth should not be termed "abandoned," because they are still intermingled with afflictions that have not yet been severed.
If one follows this reasoning:
At the time of detachment from desire,
one is merely able to take cessation as an object; this is what is called abandonment,
not the elimination of associated afflictions.
Since this is so, when one is born as a superior sage,
even the various afflictions do not arise;
they are naturally absent.
Just as the afflictions of the path of seeing and the latent tendencies of the path of cultivation are also called "abandoned" when their binding conditions have not yet been exhausted,
once abandoned, they never arise again because their intrinsic nature is powerful.
It is said that these are abandoned;
the same should apply to the categories of wholesome dharmas and so forth,
because the afflictions that take them as objects are powerful.
Even that which does not depend on the abandonment of miscellaneous afflictions is also termed "abandonment.
This being so, one should consider how it is by virtue of this [term] that they are called "outflowing" (sāsrava). Question: Just as the five views are part of wisdom (prajñā),...
The essence of wisdom is that which should be severed;
it is not that which should be severed. That which should be severed is as follows:
That is, for dharmas associated [with the mind], there is no abandonment through dissociation from association,
because their essential nature is all susceptible to abandonment.
If they were not subject to abandonment,
then the five views would not constitute the essence of the outflows (āsrava),
nor would they constitute the essence of the fetters (bandhana).
The same applies to the questions concerning lack of clear comprehension (*asaṃprajanya*) and so forth.
Answer: Among the universal (*sarvatraga*) and object-specific (*viṣayapratiniyata*) mental factors, those whose essence is view (*dṛṣṭi*) constitute bondage.
It is not the case that they are not views, for view is that which is characterized by grasping.
Consequently, these ten [factors] exclude wisdom; all other nine factors belong to the defiled portion.
When included among the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) and so forth,
their essential nature is not that of an outflow (*āsrava*);
the name "outflow" is applied to them only figuratively.
Otherwise, there would be no bound associated phenomena such as improper mental attention (*ayoniśomanasikāra*) and so forth;
this would lead to many contradictions. Thus says the treatise.
"Second, non-arising abandonment, which leads to their never arising again.
Commentary: "Dependent upon" (*āśraya*) means "cause" (*hetu*).
It is the locus of dependence.
Because the cause lacks a basis, the effect necessarily does not arise;
because the effect lacks a basis, the cause likewise does not arise.
Treatise:
Ranging from those abandoned through seeing (*darśana-heya*) to those abandoned through cultivation alone (*bhāvanā-heya*).
Commentary: [As stated above].
Based on the aforementioned abandonment through detachment from bonds,
the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (66) states that all contaminated (*sāsrava*) wholesome states and non-obscured neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) states [are abandoned].
They are abandoned solely through cultivation;
as stated in the fifty-seventh [treatise],
the six faculties beginning with faith (śraddhā) pertain to both abandonment through cultivation and non-abandonment.

However, because these fetters take this as their object and arise in this state, they are all abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*). Question: Do not the afflictions of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) also take this as their object? Answer: They do take it as their object and do indeed arise [in relation to it].
However, because they have not yet been exhausted, they were not mentioned;
since this treatise discusses the point where they are exhausted, it speaks only of those abandoned through cultivation. Treatise: [End]
"Based on non-arising, [defilements] are abandoned up to those abandoned by vision alone.
Commentary: This refers to abandonment based on subsequent non-arising.
The *Abhidharmakośa* (Chapter 4),
the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (Section 66),
and other texts state that the eighth consciousness and so forth constitute the substantial entity of the various evil destinies (*durgati*) and the destinies of karmic maturation (*vipākagati*).
It is abandoned only by insight;
likewise, the state of non-perception and so forth are also abandoned only by insight.
Their entry through the gates of the wholesome and the indeterminate is subsumed under the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
Their entry through the gate of the extinction of dependence is exclusively abandoned by insight (*darśanaprahātavya*),
because these are merely afflictions arising from conceptual construction that give rise to [the views of] non-Buddhists and the like.
Upon entering the path of seeing,
all conceptual afflictions are severed,
as one abandons the physical body that serves as the basis for non-Buddhists and others.
Because of those such as the attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*), it also does not arise;
"such as" includes the heaven of non-conception (*asaṃjñika*), hermaphrodites (*paṇḍaka*), those with both sexual organs (*ubhayavyañjana*), the northern continent of Uttarakuru, and so forth.

However, the *Pañcavastuka* (Treatise on the Five Categories) states in fifty-three places that non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) is attained at the time of the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*).
Furthermore, that same fascicle states that the Heaven of Non-conception (*asaṃjñi-sattva*) and so forth are instances of non-analytical cessation.
As for the claim that this contradicts the present text,
it is not so; this teaching states that non-arising is also subsumed within analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
"Severance" has the meaning of relinquishment;
it does not have the meaning of being an antidote.
If that were so, then by extension, the states of the miserable realms and the fruits of evil karma would also necessarily be of an indeterminate nature.

Therefore, the Abhidharma (Dharmapada) states in its fourth [chapter] that the karma and its results pertaining to the miserable destinies (*durgati*) are abandoned through the path of vision (*darśanamārga*),
or that they are said to be abandoned through the path of vision when spoken of in conjunction with their causes.
It is not the severance of the objects of attachment, their fetters, or their seeds.
The five faculties (*indriya*) being abandoned through seeing (*darśana-prahātavya*) are also explained in this same way.
There are four kinds of abandonment, as explained according to the distinctions in meaning in the separate notes (*pṛthak-lekha*).
According to the *Nyāyānusāra*,
there are only three types: first,
abandonment by intrinsic nature (*svabhāvaprahāṇa*).
This refers to defiled phenomena.
Second is abandonment through detachment from bonds,
which refers to that which can sever the afflictions associated with those objects.
Wholesome and indeterminate dharmas are completely exhausted only when abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
Third is abandonment by way of non-arising (*anutpāda-prahāṇa*), which means severing their basis so that they never arise again.
This is of two kinds. The first refers to the disappearance of the fruit following the disappearance of the cause;
that is, the fruits of the three evil destinies are said to be abandoned through the Path of Seeing.
Because the causes— afflictions and karma— are absent,
the effects will never arise again; thus,
as the two effects are exhausted, their causes are accordingly severed.
This means that even the distinct retributions for wholesome karma within the three evil destinies are abandoned upon seeing the Path;
because the fruit which is the basis [of the afflictions] no longer exists, the cause perishes accordingly.
The non-ideational attainment (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) and other such states induce afflictions.
In the stage of seeing (*darśana-mārga*), when the cause perishes, the effect follows and is abandoned through seeing.
This applies to those of indeterminate gender (*paṇḍaka*) and others as well.
This is primarily because the afflictions of conceptualization are actively manifesting.
Upon entering the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), the cause perishes and the fruit ceases; the rest is as explained in the *Viniścaya-saṃgrahaṇī*.
How many [afflictions] pertain to the paths of seeing and cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*)?
Treatise:
It should be understood that the explanation of the twelve links [of dependent origination] is as it ought to be.
Commentary: [As follows].
Regarding the statement in the *Yogācārabhūmi* and other texts that the twelve links are common to both types of abandonment (*prahāṇa*),
one should understand them as they apply within those two types: among them,
ignorance (*avidyā*), craving (*tṛṣṇā*), and grasping (*upādāna*) are abandoned by their very nature (*svabhāva-prahāṇa*).
However, they pertain to both the paths of seeing and cultivation;
they are not mentioned because they are weak in terms of being free from bondage and non-arising.
As for formations (*saṃskāra*), a small portion pertains to all three types: intrinsic nature, freedom from bondage, and non-arising.
Defiled states abandoned through seeing and cultivation are severed by their very nature (*svabhāva-prahāṇa*).
Non-defiled states are characterized by both non-arising and liberation from bondage;
liberation from bondage can be understood [as follows].
Because the attainment of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) and so forth are abandoned by the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*),
the formations (*saṃskāra*) and existence (*bhava*) do not arise.
The seven branches beginning with consciousness (*vijñāna*) arise only when they are free from bondage.
The essence is not a defiled dharma;
it is not severed by its own nature.
This is because the miserable realms, humans, and devas should be understood according to their respective conditions. As stated in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle 10:
The stream-enterer and the once-returner sever one portion of all the factors;

Question: Among the six consciousnesses, there are also results of maturation (vipākaphala).
Why does the verse not state that the former perishes and the latter arises?
It is because the manifestation of the six consciousnesses is also not separate from consciousness itself,
as they are the fruit of maturation (*vipākaphala*).
Treatise:
Because the evolving consciousnesses are intermittent and are not maturation (*vipāka*).
Commentary says:
Because it is not a true ripening result (*vipāka*),
the six [consciousnesses] are not said to be active;
the intent of the verse refers specifically to the eighth consciousness.
This is precisely because it is the dharma of the continuous succession of birth and death.
